The technical report behind The Cliff

The Cliff: True Aging Curves by Sport and Position

When do athletes actually get old? Aging curves for 14 sport/position cells across the NFL, NBA, MLB and NHL, estimated with the naive average, the standard delta method and a player fixed-effects "career model", with a simulation that tests which estimators survive survivorship bias when players age at different rates.

Summary of findings

The cliff (one definition, used in this report and in the article): the first age after the peak at which aging has cost the typical player half a standard deviation of talent, where the talent SD is the spread of the persistent player effect among players with two or more qualifying seasons, net of season-to-season noise (Curve to cliff). It is the drop that turns a player better than about 7 in 10 established players at his position into an average one (for NFL running backs, 2.2 fpts/gm, roughly the gap between the RB12 and the RB21 by fpts/gm in a typical 2015-2025 season). Because it is measured in talent units, it is comparable across metrics and sports. "Share of peak" and "the 80% line" are reported separately for volume statistics and are never called the cliff.

1. Naive averages hide the decline; the two honest estimators bracket the truth. In all 14 cells with data at 33, the naive average shows less decline than the career model. The delta method shows more decline than the career model in all 14. In the simulation (Simulation), the career model is right when every player ages on the same schedule and runs up to 1 year late when decline rates differ between players (which the real data show they do, Aging rates); the delta method runs 0.7 to 1.7 years early when everyone ages alike. In every one of 11 simulated scenarios (12 leagues each), the true cliff age lay inside the bracket formed by the two, and a stress test with 12 further cases (Stress test: decline-rate spreads up to 2.3 times the average, a doubled star link, flatter and steeper curves) agreed, with two limits: at the noise level of goalies and relievers the bracket missed 25% of leagues when everyone aged alike (with decline rates that also vary, as they do in the real data, it held in all 8, Noise and heterogeneity), and the bracket is a property of an early threshold (at 0.75 SD it fails under strong heterogeneity). So the headline is a bracket: delta method = fast end, career model = slow end.

2. Running backs fall first. NFL RBs peak at 24 (95% CI 23 to 26) and reach the cliff at 29 on both estimators (delta 29 (28 to 30), career model 29 (28 to 31)). On the proportional models, a typical back at 30 keeps 55% to 74% of his peak production.

3. Most football positions and the NBA go over at 30 or 31; quarterbacks and hockey skaters later. Cliff brackets: WR 30 to 31, TE 30 to 31, DB 30, LB 30 to 31, DL 31, NBA 30 to 31, QB 32 to 33, NHL forwards 32 to 33, NHL defensemen 32 to 34.

4. Baseball and goalies age, but their cliff is hard to pin down. Brackets: MLB hitters 30 to 34, starters 27 to 31, relievers 28 to 33, NHL goalies 26 to 30. How much the slow end should be favoured depends on how noisy the season statistic is relative to the talent spread (season residual SD / talent-SD, Metrics): goalies 1.84, relievers 1.65, starters 1.37, hitters 1.09 (NFL QB 0.99, DB 1.05). At goalie and reliever noise (1.66 in the stress test) the delta method ran 2.8 years early and the career model 0.2 years early; with decline-rate spreads of 1.4 and 2.3 added, the delta method ran about 2.2 years early and the career model 0.5 to 1.2 years late (Noise and heterogeneity). The slow end is therefore the closer point estimate for goalies and relievers, and more weakly for starters, but it can itself be up to about a year late: goalies 29 to 30, relievers 32 to 33, starters 30 to 31. Hitters' noise is like a quarterback's; at that level the delta method runs about a year early and hitters' decline-rate spread (1.4) makes the career model about a year late, so the simulation cannot pick an end: the hitter cliff is 30 to 34, most plausibly 31 to 33. v0.1's statement that baseball "barely has a cliff" and that goalies and relievers "never reach 80%" was an artifact of index units and is withdrawn.

5. For fantasy, age adds to regression; stars lose more points, and outside running backs about the same share. Top-24 RBs aged 27-28 give back 3.2 fpts/gm (PPR fantasy points per game) the next season (95% CI 2.5 to 3.9), 1.2 more than young starters. Backs in the top quarter at ages 23-25 lose 5.2 fpts/gm from 26 to 30, the rest 1.8 (Star tiers, tiers fixed before the ages measured).

Units. fpts = PPR fantasy points (nflverse fantasy_points_ppr); fpts/gm = per game with a stat line. Talent-SD: Curve to cliff. CIs are 95% player-bootstrap percentile intervals; they cover sampling error only, and the spread between estimators (reported next to them) is usually larger.

Question, definitions, metrics

The question: at what age does the typical player's production start to fall, how fast does it fall, and how does that compare across positions and sports? The complication is survivorship. A player only produces a statistic while a team keeps playing him, and teams stop playing players who decline. Any curve built from observed seasons is built from the players who were still good enough to be observed.

Age

Age is an integer: completed years on a league-specific reference date, so that a player's age rises by exactly one per season. The reference dates are listed below.

LeagueAge measured onWhy
NFLSeptember 1 of the seasonnflverse convention; the season starts in September
NBAFebruary 1 of the season's ending yearBasketball-Reference convention (mid-season)
MLBJune 30 of the seasonBaseball-Reference convention (mid-season)
NHLFebruary 1 of the season's ending yearHockey-Reference convention (mid-season)

Metrics and playing-time thresholds

Each cell uses one primary production metric where more is better, and a season qualifies when the player cleared a playing-time threshold. Thresholds are scaled to season length where noted (strikes, lockouts, COVID), and volume metrics are rescaled so every season's qualifying average equals the average of the league's last five seasons. The talent-SD column is the yardstick for the cliff; the last column is the season-to-season residual SD divided by it, a measure of how noisy one season is relative to the talent spread (used in Stress test to match simulated noise levels to real cells).

Definitions. fpts: PPR fantasy points (nflverse fantasy_points_ppr: 1 per reception, 0.1 per rushing or receiving yard, 6 per rushing or receiving TD, 0.04 per passing yard, 4 per passing TD, 2 per two-point conversion, −2 per interception or fumble lost); fpts/gm divides by games with a stat line. Two-point conversions matter at the margin: Gurley's 2018 total of 372.1 includes three. IDP points: solo tackle 1, assist 0.5, tackle for loss 1, sack 3, QB hit 0.5, interception 3, pass defended 1, forced fumble 2, fumble recovery 2, defensive TD 6, safety 2; per game with a defensive snap. Defense is analysed for 2013-2025 only: nflverse's 2012 snap-count file is empty (checked again in September 2026, CSV and parquet), so 2013 is the first season with defensive playing time. Game Score (Hollinger): PTS + 0.4 FGM − 0.7 FGA − 0.4 (FTA − FTM) + 0.7 ORB + 0.3 DRB + STL + 0.7 AST + 0.7 BLK − 0.4 PF − TOV. OPS+ = 100 (OBP / lgOBP + SLG / lgSLG − 1), league = AL or NL that season excluding pitchers' batting, with no park factor (so it differs slightly from Baseball-Reference, for example Bonds 2004: 264.5 here, 263 there). FIP index = 200 − 100 FIP / lgERA (100 = average, higher is better). Goals-against index = 100 (2 − (1 − sv%) / (1 − league sv%)).

Why talent-SDs. v0.1 compared sports on "share of peak", the level at an age divided by the average qualifying player's level at the peak age. That is not a common currency. On an index (OPS+, FIP index, GA index) zero is arbitrary, so 80% of 100 is far below replacement; and on a counting stat the anchor is the average qualifier, mostly backups, so the same loss in points is a bigger share. v0.2 measures declines in units of the between-player talent spread, which is comparable across all 14 cells, and reports share of peak only for volume statistics, from proportional (log) models that need no anchor and cannot go below zero.

The estimators, step by step

Notation: mi,a is player i's metric in the season he is age a; Qa is the set of qualifying seasons at age a; Pa the set of survivor pairs (qualifying at a and at a+1, consecutive seasons). Every estimator produces a yearly step Δ(a), the expected change from age a to a+1, and a curve S chained from those steps.

Naive average by age

L(a) = (1 / |Q_a|) Σ_(i in Q_a) m_(i,a) Δ_naive(a) = L(a+1) − L(a)

This compares different people at different ages. At 34 it averages only the players who are still employed at 34, who are disproportionately the ones who never declined. It is biased toward a late, flat curve.

Standard delta method

Δ_delta(a) = (1 / |P_a|) Σ_(i in P_a) ( m_(i,a+1) − m_(i,a) ) S(a_0) = 0, S(a+1) = S(a) + Δ(a)

Comparing the same player with himself removes differences in talent, which is why analysts have used it for two decades. Its weakness is who enters Pa: a pair exists only if the player qualified in both seasons. Teams keep players partly on last season's numbers, and last season contains luck, so the kept players' age-a seasons are luckier than their talent and regress the next year: the method books that regression as aging (too steep). At the same time, if some players decline faster than others, the fast decliners are cut first, so the pairs at older ages over-represent slow agers (too flat). The primary version counts each pair once; the classic harmonic-mean playing-time weighting is reported in Other corrections.

Career model (player fixed effects)

In plain terms. Imagine two running backs. Back A plays from 24 to 29 and averages 15 fpts a game. Back B plays from 22 to 25 and averages 8. At 28 only Back A is left, so the naive "average 28-year-old" is 15 and backs appear to improve with age. The career model avoids that. First it works out each player's own normal (A: 15, B: 8). Then, for every season, it asks how far above or below his own normal the player was. Averaging those personal gaps by age gives the age effect, and it no longer matters that only good players remain at 28, because each season is measured against its own player. A player's "normal" is itself built from seasons at different ages, so the model alternates: re-estimate the normals with the age effects removed, then the age effects with the normals removed, until neither changes. Why it beats the delta method on luck: the delta method's baseline is the previous season, which was often lucky (that is partly why the player was kept); the career model's baseline is the whole career, where one lucky year is one input among several. What it cannot fix: if players decline at different rates, the players still observed at 33 are the slow decliners, and the model reads their slope as everyone's. That is why it is the slow end of the bracket.
m_(i,a) = α_i + β_a + e_(i,a) for every qualifying season of every player Δ_fe(a) = β_(a+1) − β_a

αi is the player's own level and βa the common age effect. Fitted by alternating projections (until the largest change is below 10−9), which is exact least squares for the two-way model; a direct least-squares check agrees to 10−4 in all 14 cells.

Variants added in v0.2

fe_log the career model on log(m), rows with m > 0: proportional aging. share of peak(a) = exp(S(a) − S(p)). No anchor, never below zero. Volume metrics only (an index has no natural zero). delta_log the delta method on log(m): mean log(m_(a+1) / m_a) over survivor pairs with both seasons > 0. fe_rt career model with personal decline rates: m = α_i + β_a + γ_i (a − K)_+ + e, K = peak + 1, with a ridge penalty λ Σ γ_i², λ = s²_e / s²_γ estimated from the within-player post-K slopes (a random-slope model with player fixed levels).

Share of nonpositive seasons dropped by the log models: at most 0.5% in any cell.

From a curve to the cliff

Every chained curve is smoothed 1-2-1 (endpoints 2-1) before summary ages are read, identically for all estimators and for the simulated truth. Then:

peak p = argmax_a S(a) talent-SD = sqrt( var(α_hat_i) − mean(s²_e / n_i) ), players with 2+ qualifying seasons, point fit prime = ages from the peak to the last age within 0.2 talent-SD of it (career model) drop_sd(a) = ( max level − level(a) ) / talent-SD CLIFF = first a > p with drop_sd(a) ≥ 0.5 share of peak = exp(S(a) − S(p)) from fe_log / delta_log (volume metrics) 80% line = first a > p with share of peak ≤ 80%

Whose spread? The talent-SD is measured among established players (2+ qualifying seasons), and cuts truncate the talent distribution, so it is smaller than the spread among everyone who enters a league. Run on the simulated leagues, the same estimator returns 0.81 of the true SD in every stress case (Stress test). So the real-data cliff is half an SD among established players, about 0.4 SD of all entrants, which puts it roughly a year earlier than a definition based on all entrants would. The deflation is stable across scenarios, so comparisons between cells are unaffected; Thresholds and eras shows the cliff at other thresholds, including 0.5 / 0.8.

"n.r." means a threshold is not reached inside the estimated age range; tables print the last age of that range, e.g. "n.r.(34)". Uncertainty, in plain terms: we re-ran everything 500 times, each time on a random re-draw of players (some drawn twice, some left out, all of a player's seasons moving together). The middle 95% of those answers is the range we report. The talent-SD is held at its point value across re-draws.

Which estimator can be trusted? A simulation with a known answer

With real data there is no ground truth, so the estimators were tested on simulated players whose true aging curve we set. In numbered steps:

  1. We create 6,000 fake players per league. Each gets a true talent level and a true aging curve (peak at 26). In some scenarios everyone shares one curve; in others each player gets his own decline rate after the peak.
  2. Each season, a player's stat line = talent + his age effect + luck (a preseason-visible part and an in-season part).
  3. Fake teams decide who plays next year using what real teams use: last year's stats (discounted for luck), the player's expected aging, and a private preseason read. Players also retire, get hurt, or get benched mid-season.
  4. We hide the truth, hand each estimator only the seasons that got played, and measure how far its answer lands.
  5. We repeat under 11 team and aging behaviors, 12 leagues each.

The scenarios, in words:

Two truths are scored. The population curve is the average aging of everyone who entered the league, had they all kept playing: the answer to "when do athletes get old?". The still-playing curve is, at each age, the average true next-year change of the players who actually have a qualifying season at that age: the answer to "what will one more year do to a player who is still in the league?". The two are identical when everyone ages alike. The first table is the error in the cliff age (years; + = too late), averaged over 12 leagues.

Reading. (a) The naive average is always late, by up to 7 years. (b) Every phantom-season rule and IPW over-corrects: the phantom is built from the dropout's last observed season, which is unluckily low. (c) When everyone ages alike, the career model is essentially exact (its cliff error is zero in all five) and the delta method runs early (−1.7 to −0.7 years); in the hidden scenario the delta method has the lower curve error, as in v0.1. (d) When decline rates differ, the career model's cliff runs up to 1 year late and it badly understates the population's decline at 33 (by 1.4 talent-SDs at worst): the players still observed at 33 are the slow agers. The delta method's two biases (luck, steep; slow-ager selection, flat) roughly cancel there, so it has the lowest population-curve error in 4 of 11 scenarios. It is right for the wrong reasons, and neither estimator is reliable for "how far down is the whole cohort at 33". (e) The cliff age is robust: it lay inside the delta–career-model bracket in every simulated league. (f) The career model with personal decline rates (fe_rt) was built to fix (d). It helps only a little on the population curve, so it is not the headline; but it has the lowest error against the still-playing curve in 10 of 11 scenarios, which makes it the right tool for the aging step in the fantasy table in Fantasy.

Tier check (Star tiers design). Splitting simulated players by their production at 23-25 and fitting ages 26+ only recovers the true 26-to-30 decline for both tiers when everyone ages alike (estimate / truth: top quarter 1.01, rest 1.07); with random decline rates both tiers are understated by the same amount (0.87 and 0.86), so the comparison between tiers stays fair. The v0.1 tiers (defined by being a fantasy starter by 26) were not.

Integer ages: the simulated truth is a symmetric peak at 26 on a one-year grid, so an average bias of 0.0 reflects the resolution of the grid as much as precision. Code: 06_simulation.py. Every drafted player gets a first season; there is no entry bar.

Stress test of the bracket (new in v0.3)

The eleven scenarios share one true curve (peak 26, true cliff 30, or 29 with injuries), and their heterogeneous cases use a decline-rate spread of 0.8, at the low end of the real 0.7 to 3.4. 06b_sim_stress.py reruns the same code on 12 cases, 4 leagues each, including the real median spread (1.4), the MLB-starter level (2.3), a doubled star link, a very noisy statistic matched to goalies and relievers, and flatter and steeper true curves, and scores the bracket at four thresholds. Each cell: share of leagues with the truth inside the delta-to-career-model bracket (inclusive), then the mean true/delta/career-model cliff age. "Rates" = spread of personal decline rates relative to the average decline. Reading. At the headline threshold the bracket held in 11 of 12 cases, including the real median heterogeneity and above. Its limits: (1) at goalie and reliever noise (1.66) it held in 75% of leagues, the career model itself running slightly early (−0.25 years); (2) with strong heterogeneity the delta method also runs late for deeper drops, so at 0.75 SD or more the bracket fails in the "Rates 2.3x (MLB starters)" and "Stars age slower, 2x link" cases: the bracket is a property of an early threshold; (3) because the true cliff is 29 to 31 in every case, the integer grid is coarse and the career model often ties the truth, so "coverage" is partly "delta at or below 30 and the career model at 30"; the 11 x 12 leagues are not 132 independent truths. On the estimated-SD yardstick every case covers except "Stars age slower, 2x link". Tier check under "stars age slower" (doubled link): estimate / truth = 0.92 for the top quarter and 0.59 for the rest. The design then overstates the gap between tiers, but dividing the real RB drops (Star tiers) by those ratios still leaves top-quarter backs losing more points (5.7 vs 3.1 fpts/gm).

Noise and heterogeneity together (new in v0.4)

The "very noisy" case above has no decline-rate heterogeneity, yet real pitchers differ in how fast they decline (starters 2.3x, Aging rates), which pushes the career model late. 06c_sim_noisy_rates.py reruns that case (it reproduces the row above exactly) and adds it combined with decline-rate spreads of 1.4x and 2.3x, 4 leagues each. Cells as above.

Reading. With heterogeneity added, the headline bracket held in all 8 leagues. The delta method stays about 2.2 years early and the career model moves to 0.5 to 1.2 years late, so the slow end is still the closer of the two, but the truth can sit a year inside it. That is why Summary 4 and the article give goalies, relievers and starters a one-year window at the slow end rather than the slow end itself. At 0.75 SD and deeper the 2.3x case fails again, as in Stress test.

Worked example: Todd Gurley through all three estimators

Gurley is a useful case because he is everything the estimators disagree about: an early star, a sharp fall, and a disappearance. Below are his seasons, what each estimator does with them, and the career-model quantities. fpts/gm are shown raw and after the era adjustment (the adjusted value is what enters the models).

Naive. Gurley's 23.3 at 24 is one of 394 qualifying RB seasons averaged into L(24) = 7.76. At 27 he is simply absent; L(27) = 8.27 is computed from 259 other backs. His collapse never shows up in the naive curve.

Delta. Five consecutive qualifying pairs enter: 21→22 (−4.42), 22→23 (+12.53), 23→24 (−1.51), 24→25 (−9.75), and 25→26 (−3.21). His 26→27 step does not exist (status "gone"), so the method never learns what age 27 did to him. The 24→25 pair books the whole −9.75 as aging at 24, although his 23 and 24 seasons were far above his career level.

Career model. Fitting the two-way model on all 2,559 qualifying RB seasons from 730 players gives Gurley a career level (α) of 16.3 fpts a game: his expected output at the reference age (20), with each other age adding that age's effect on top. Residuals show that 23 and 24 were +7.5 and +6.0 above his own level, and 26 was −6.7 below it.

What the model gets wrong about him. Gurley's decline came with a chronic knee condition: a permanent, player-specific shock. The career model treats his 26 as mostly bad luck against a stable career level, which is exactly the heterogeneous-aging case in Simulation where it runs slow. His case is an argument for the bracket, not for either end of it.

The chart plots the same three things by age: Gurley's actual seasons, what the career model expects from him (his own level plus the league-wide RB age effect), and the naive average he is being compared with.

Figure 3. Gurley's era-adjusted fpts/gm against the career-model fitted path and the naive RB average at each age. Labels: career-model residuals, which the model reads as luck. Tap to open full size.

Surprises, honestly reported. (a) The naive curve does not just flatten decline, it can invert it: naive NHL forwards "peak" at 40 and naive WRs at 35. (b) QB fpts/gm has no sharp peak: the career model's point peak is 24 with an interval of 24 to 30, and passing efficiency (EPA per dropback, Secondary metrics) peaks later. One likely reason: young quarterbacks run more, and rushing points fade first. (c) In talent units, pitchers and goalies age like everyone else; v0.1's "never reach 80%" for relievers and goalies was a property of index units. (d) The additive career model goes slightly below zero for the NBA at the oldest ages (minimum share −16%); the proportional model cannot, and both are extrapolations on thin samples there.

The fantasy table (NFL QB, RB, WR, TE)

Two different numbers answer two different questions. The aging step is what one more year does to a player who is still in the league, from the career model with personal decline rates (the best estimator for the still-playing curve in Simulation; the plain career-model step is shown next to it). The starter outcome is what actually happened the next season to fantasy starters at that age (top-24 RB and WR, top-12 QB and TE by season PPR total), which includes regression to the mean. Starred rows have fewer than 40 starters (the same thin-sample rule as the curves). The article's cheat sheet uses the starter outcomes, which fans experience directly, with missed seasons counted as zero; the aging step is the cleaner estimate of age alone and agrees in direction (RB −0.85 at 27, −0.97 at 28).

Do stars age differently?

v0.1 split players by whether they were ever a fantasy starter by 26, which selects on outcomes (a star who faded early is less likely to qualify) and gave a misleading "same schedule" reading. v0.2 fixes the tier before the ages being measured: players are split by their average production over qualifying seasons at 23-25 (top quarter vs the rest), and the career model is fitted on their seasons at 26 and older only. Simulation shows this design is unbiased when everyone ages alike. The table gives the level at 26, the drop from 26 to 30 in the metric's units (95% CI), and the level at 30 as a share of the level at 26. Decimals follow the unit: 1 for fpts/gm, IDP/gm and Game Score, 0 for OPS+ and the pitching and goalie indices, 2 for NHL points per game.

Receivers match the band rule: the first single age with a full-point extra drop is 29, so the drop lands in the age-30 season. Running backs do not quite: starters aged 27 give back an extra 0.6 (−1.9 to +0.7), starters aged 28 an extra 2.2 (−3.5 to −0.7). The pooled 27-28 band puts the RB sell-by at the age-28 season; one age at a time, the big drop lands in the age-29 season. The article therefore calls the winter before the age-28 season the safe sell and the winter before the age-29 season the last call. Single ages from 27 to 30 rest on 26 to 72 starters and the intervals overlap, so this is a refinement, not a second finding.

The zero-game seasons behind the TE 31+ band (6 of 44 starter seasons) are mostly retirements after a starting season (reasons hand-checked on Wikipedia): Tony Gonzalez (2013, age 37: retired); Shannon Sharpe (2003, age 35: retired); Jason Witten (2017, age 35: retired, returned 2019); Benjamin Watson (2015, age 34: injury: Achilles, 2016 preseason); Rob Gronkowski (2021, age 32: retired); Dennis Pitta (2016, age 31: injury: hip, 2017; released). For a redraft manager a retirement is known before the draft; for a dynasty or keeper manager it is a zero. The RB 29+ zeros: Tiki Barber (2006, age 31: retired); Corey Dillon (2006, age 31: retired); James Stewart (2002, age 30: no 2003 games, reason not verified); Dominic Rhodes (2008, age 29: unsigned, returned 2010); Michael Turner (2012, age 30: released, unsigned); DeMarco Murray (2017, age 29: retired).

Do players age at different rates?

The heterogeneous-aging scenarios in Simulation rest on this. For players with 4+ qualifying seasons at 27-33, a straight line through each player's seasons (after removing the common age effect) gives his personal slope; the spread of those slopes minus sampling noise estimates the true spread of decline rates. The last column compares it with the average yearly decline over 28-33.

The spread of decline rates is 0.7 to 3.4 times the average decline (median 1.4): at least as large as in the simulation's "random decline rates" scenario (0.8), and the stress test (Stress test) shows the bracket still holds at the median (1.4) and at 2.3. Real aging is heterogeneous, which is why the headline is a bracket.

Players behind the curves

These lists are generated by rule, not picked by hand (10_examples.py). Early cliffs: fantasy starters (top quartile elsewhere) aged 26+ whose next season fell to 60% or less of it, or who had no usable next season. Injuries are included on purpose, because a lost season is part of what age does; Tom Brady's 2008 (one game, torn ACL) is the clearest example of a "cliff" that was not aging. Long primes: players whose best qualifying season came at 30+ (RB 29+, other leagues 32+) and ranked in the top fifth that season, or who stayed at 90%+ of their best past 33 (other leagues 35). New in v0.2: only players whose debut is inside the data (first season after the data's first year, or first seen at 23 or younger), so careers that began before the data cannot produce a false "best at 33"; "(active)" marks players still playing in the last data season. The rule has a hole: a veteran who was absent from the data's first season (minor leagues, injury) passes it. Dwayne Roloson is the example: he spent 2000-01 in the AHL, so his first NHL season in the data is 2001-02 although he debuted earlier. His row is kept because his 2003-04 is genuinely his career best, but a real debut year (draft or first-season fields) would be the stricter rule. Values are raw, not era-adjusted.

Limitations

  • The answer is a bracket because the key assumption cannot be tested from inside the data. Whether players who left would have declined faster than those who stayed is exactly what the data cannot show. The simulation says the true cliff age lies between the delta method and the career model across the scenarios we could imagine; a world with even stronger selection on decline rates than we simulated could push it outside. The simulation also has one true curve (true cliff 30, or 29), an inclusive integer bracket in which the career model often ties the truth, coverage of only 75% at goalie and reliever noise when everyone ages alike (full coverage once decline rates also vary, Noise and heterogeneity), and no coverage at thresholds of 0.75 SD or more under strong heterogeneity (Stress test).
  • The yardstick is measured among established players. The talent-SD comes from players with 2+ qualifying seasons, which shrinks it (about 0.81 of the entrants' SD in simulation), so the cliff sits about a year earlier than an all-entrants definition would put it. The order of the cells is unaffected (Thresholds and eras).
  • How far down the whole cohort is at 33 is not well identified. With heterogeneous aging, both estimators understate the population's decline at old ages (Simulation). Statements about 33+ describe the players who are still playing.
  • Functional form. The additive and proportional models agree on the cliff ages but differ on share of peak (RB at 30: additive 62%, proportional 55% to 74%); the tiers (Star tiers) favour proportional.
  • Production mixes role and ability. fpts/gm, Game Score and points per game fall when coaches cut touches and minutes, which is what fantasy players experience but not pure physical decline (Secondary metrics).
  • Age and era are entangled. With a player effect, age and calendar year are nearly collinear, so the model cannot also include season effects. Volume metrics are rescaled by league-season; the rescale factor is the qualifying mean, which moves with that season's age mix (Thresholds and eras tests a factor from ages 25-29 only). League-relative indices (OPS+, FIP index, GA index) drift down for a fixed-ability player as the league improves, which adds a small period trend to aging.
  • Left truncation. Tested (Thresholds and eras, "Debut in data"): headline cliffs move by a year or less. NFL defense past about 31 is identified mainly by veterans who were already mid-career in 2013.
  • Coverage. NFL defense 2013-2025 (no 2012 snap counts); NFL targets missing 2003-2008 (receptions used); NBA ends in 2022-23 (an incomplete season: 1,176 of 1,230 games, absorbed by the season-length scaling) and MLB in 2021 although newer seasons exist upstream; NBA birth dates from ESPN (7 of 2,257 ids had no date).
  • Fantasy table. Starter outcomes are descriptive and include regression to the mean; bands past 30 rest on few players.

Reproducibility

Run the scripts in order from ebk-age-cliff/scripts. Python 3.12 with pandas, numpy, matplotlib, pyarrow and openpyxl; no statsmodels or scikit-learn. Seeds are fixed. Everything after step 01 runs offline (about 15 minutes on a laptop). v0.1 scripts and tables are archived in scripts/_v01 and outputs/_v01, v0.2 scripts in scripts/_v02; v0.3 builders in scripts/_v03; the change logs are reports/changelog_c1.md, changelog_c2.md and changelog_c3.md.

The Cliff

Running backs go over it at 29. Hockey skaters hang on until 32 or later. Both ages come from rebuilding the aging curves for 14 position groups in four leagues, this time counting the players who quietly vanished from the data.
